I have been playing these games for quite awhile. Though mostly on my phone as I have the app downloaded there as well. There are only 5 games for this Steam version and one you HAVE to pay $6.99 to unlock (so 4 are included as is) which I don't like. What should have been done is a "let me play anyway and wait" instead of forcing the premium upload. Covenant is free in the app. In the mobile version, you have access to a lot more and for some reason they have achievements for the ones not on the app currently (unless they become visible when you pay $6.99) so did they want you to use the mobile app and transfer achievements? 

I have given them money by buying stars and keys so I am not 100% opposed, but I am using this app purely for achievements from the mobile version so I am annoyed that I can no longer get achievements for the remaining games. 

Here is how this game works in general: 

1. You start out with 2 keys. 

2. Each chapter requires 1 key to unlock to download and play

3. When you run out of keys, you wait 3 hours for one key or 6 hours for both! Not the worst and you can watch ads to take 30 minutes off the timer.. though they do eventually stop you... best to do this when you are on Chapter 6. 

4. Most stories have 8 chapters, though one game (that I count) and most of the games brought over from the standalone apps before they prioritized this app have 10 chapters!

If you fully refuse to buy anything even slightly adjacent or related to microtransactions than you can on average beat 1 story per day depending on when you start it, how smart you are, how clueless you are at noticing hidden things to pick up and how late you stay up or how much time you have for this kind of thing. Which isn't all that horrible. I did buy a few of the stars for skips (cause I use a guide cause I am a proud dumbass who is dumb as fuck) and keys! 

I found the stories engaging for what this was, and I have downloaded all of the apps I can. Even the first game they worked on! I love these. The art is fantastic. I even enjoyed the music loops that they play (Pirate's Treasure had the worst one but it was good white noise) and wish these developers introduced a music player so that we can listen to completed background music. Or release it to youtube... Many people might not agree, but I wish it was an option.

Though some times not completely intuitive, this game presents the player with puzzles which can be solved using careful observation of the puzzle, the available rooms and creativity. Each chapter consists of a several puzzles which may take several hours to solve.  Each chapter is locked by a key.  Each key takes 3 hours to generate after use.  Which for me is fine as it takes roughly that amount of time to finish a chapter.  The game stores up to 2 keys for the player.

Overall it's a well executed point and click adventure with tens of hours of content available for play across 4 or more stories.  Worth checking out!

PS:  There is a hint function in game in case the player gets stuck on a particular puzzle.  Hints are limited and additional hits are rewarded as puzzles and chapters are solved.

Игра "Adventure Escape Mysteries" - это прекрасная коллекция квестов, объединяющая интересные сюжеты, сложные головоломки и приятную графику. Каждая история предлагает уникальную атмосферу, будь то заброшенный особняк, древний храм или космический корабль. Головоломки довольно разнообразны и заставляют хорошенько подумать, но при этом не кажутся нерешаемыми, что делает процесс прохождения увлекательным и захватывающим. Отлично реализована система подсказок, позволяющая не застрять надолго в одном месте, если возникают трудности. Персонажи, хоть и схематичные, но достаточно интересные, чтобы сопереживать им. Разработчики регулярно выпускают новые истории, что поддерживает интерес к игре на долгое время. Единственный минус - некоторая линейность сюжета, но это компенсируется интересными головоломками и захватывающей атмосферой каждой истории. В целом, "Adventure Escape Mysteries" - отличный выбор для любителей квестов и головоломок, желающих провести время с удовольствием и пользой для ума. Рекомендую!

Not sure if I paid money for this, but its exactly what it says on the tin. Perhaps you're trying to maintain a certain level of cognitive function, or you just like a game that requires you to actively engage with its contents. This is what you download for that. If it costs money then I'd recommend the app, apparently it still actively receives new content. Either way, there's a lot of content in this version as well, easily 50 stories. 

Variety of experiences: Each setting is a distinct, despite doing many of the same things over and over they don't feel same-y. So far haven't seen the same mini-game twice. There's an overarching narrative, which it didn't need, but I personally find it charming seeing reoccurring characters at different stages of their respective journeys. The narrative is expanded upon non-linearly. With certain exceptions no story directly continues from another story, but they all exist in the same history and world. The game expects you play the easiest levels first and gradually increase in difficulty overtime, but you can play in whatever order you chose.  

The key hook system: Each level is about 30-60min of playtime.  Each level is 1/8th of a story. You need keys to access levels. Every 3 hours you receive 1 key for a maximum of 2. If you're hypersensitive to that sort of thing, or want to play 8 hours a day, this isn't the game for you.

To unlock the next chapter in an adventure, you need one key. You can buy keys, or wait 3 hours. you might think that's not too bad, since you can just let the keys come in overnight, but that isn't true. It only gives 3 hours for another key if it has less than 2. Two keys or more won't generate any more keys until you spend one. Luckily though, the prices for buying keys are pretty cheap.

It's a point-and-click adventure game with puzzles. And it's free. What more could you want? I've seen reviewers complain about the key system and, fair point, if you REALLY wanted to binge any of the storylines in a single sitting (or if you really suck at solving puzzles...) you'll have to resort to microtransactions. But if you're just looking for an hour or possibly two hours of gameplay a night, you can have that at no cost whatsoever. Highly recommended for fans of the genre.

I gotta say, for a game bundle that is functionally free, these are fantastic.

I got hooked quickly. The puzzles are, for the most part, very intuitive. You're generally given enough clues to be able to solve them, and there's no complicated crafting system for combining items. In terms of buying hints, the star points system is resource management rather than a penalty; it's very easy to stockpile earned stars since the majority of puzzles are reasonable to solve on your own. For certain puzzles, if you have 30 stars, you can even skip them entirely.

Having to wait for keys to regenerate so that I can unlock more chapters is a bit annoying on weekends, but it offers me a natural stopping point on weeknights. Most of the chapters have enough content in them that it doesn't just feel like a cheap trick to get you to pay for more keys (though the earlier games are worse when it comes to intuitiveness and content amount). I can understand the developer needing to hold back players from just consuming ALL the content at once considering it's GOOD content that *can* be played entirely for free if you're patient enough.

Pro Tip: If you're ever feeling lost on what your objective is, check the title of the hint box. It'll usually clue you in on what puzzle you should be working on solving.

--

Editing to add individual game opinions (spoiler-free):

- Something I discovered after finished this bundle via desktop is there's even more individual games by the developer available in the iOS app store. That led me to discover that some of the adventures in this bundle set were repurposed from the app store games. When played individually on the app, there's no paywalling--the chapters are short with barely any content per chapter BUT they're all unlocked. Games such as Midnight Carnival and Haunted Hunt are annoying to play within the bundle because they weren't originally made with a paywall in mind.

- I will say about Haunted Hunt that it has a fantastic magic system and a super compelling story. Using the shapeshifting is integral to solving the puzzles in a very interesting way.

- On the flip side, Cursed Crown was frustrating for me. The magic system feels tacked on in a way that you forget to use it. Neither the story nor the characters were particularly compelling either.

- I love Mirror Man. There's a nice variety of puzzles, and it never felt stale for me. The horror flavor is nice too (I've already devoured every Rusty Lake game), and if you can handle occasional jump scares (which are just there to give you a little controlled scare without asking for a response), you should be fine with this one

- I hate Allied Spies. Many of the puzzles are either timed or require timing. Too much reliance on reflexes. I had to use up a LOT of stars to skip puzzles that were just effing impossible for me to manage

- Legend of the Stones duology is mehhhhh. Very repetitive puzzles with the board pieces and then the boss battles. The latter of which is timed. I had to skip many of the boss battles because I just couldn't handle it

- The Detective Kate series is decent. It's a whole lot of copaganda, but if you can get past that, the puzzles are reasonable for a straight-forward murder mystery series. Chapter lengths vary wildly though. But I can say the Trapmaker adventures are fun since it gives an excuse for literal escape rooms.

- Painted Worlds has some mechanics and puzzles that are unique to itself, and I mostly enjoyed it. There was ONE puzzle that required clicking the screen in a reflex test that couldn't be skipped, and it was so frustrating that I rage quit for a while. I had to switch my setup from touchpad to a mouse just to get past it. 

- The Squire's Tale surprised me with how much I didn't hate it. The first chapter has a puzzle-battle against some goblins, and I was worried this would be a core mechanic throughout the adventure. Thankfully it's not so! I was also very pleased that the final boss battle was not reflex-based. 

- Adventures that I enjoyed, though I don't have any specific commentary on them: Psychic Squad, The Sultan's Inventor, Lost Ruins series 

- The Puzzle Pack is just 6 of the same puzzles for every chapter, which gets monotonous after a while. Supposedly it offers guidance/Easter Eggs for the Covenant, but that information slid right off of me

- Covenant is the only paid game (hints are free and chapters all unlocked). After having gone through hundreds of hours playing everything else, I paid for it as a gift to the developers. And given how short the chapters are and how horrible a few of the puzzles end up being, I don't think the game itself is worth the $7. For example, the final "boss battle" is an arcade style mini-game (boo hiss) that does not function as a puzzle. There's also TWO puzzle hints in the game that require AUDIO, which makes them non-accessible to deaf/HoH people and anyone like me, who turned off all audio for personal reasons and was like wtf is going on. With all that said, at least the game offers some replay-ability based on the NPCs you choose, which changes the flavor of the ending and varies up how much background information you learn.

Overall, my experience with this game was very positive. The first story I chose to begin with was the "Trapmaker" series at it appeared to be captivating and interesting based off of the description of the first EP as well as the visual art covers for the 3 separate acts. As expected, it did not let me down and had me on a wild journey that had me glued to the edge of my seat with each puzzle I solved in order to progress the story along. It was a creative take on the who-done-it genera in EP 1. Following that act, it was a complex chase after trapmaker in acts 2 and 3. Many of the puzzles in this story was exciting and thrilling to solve, being very reminiscent of Jigsaw and the "Saw" franchise. The light sprinkles of humor, mixed with the right music in the background made these puzzles very interactive and captivating through and through. The same can be said for the other story I played. The pirate themed story had a great premise and did not rely too heavily on the movie cliches. This story felt like a great mix of various elements from the "Indian of Jones" series and "Pirates of the Caribbean" into one package. This story was not long, but also not too short. The music fit the story very well and helped to further immerse into this world of pirates and scallywags.

Despite this, there are a few huge critiques that makes me feel like this game format was also aimed to copy games that was more focused on revenue instead of overall satisfaction and enjoyment. What I am referring to is the difficulty of many of the puzzles both in the "Trapmaker" and "Pirate Cove" stories. Various of the puzzles from both stories is too complex for someone to just figure out without hints or help. You are given in-game currency to help when you need, but when you run out of this currency you must buy more. This also is the same for unlocking EPs in the game. You have a max of 3 keys over a very long time. Each key to unlock an EP is set at a timer of 2 hours, which in my opinion is way too long of a wait, unless they were thinking that is how long it would take to solve and complete each EP. Although I get the incentive for there being some form of payment in a free-to-play puzzle game, these types of forced payments makes it very difficult to completely defend the enjoyability of the game. I really do enjoy the conepts and stories they went for, but this form of money making is very frustrating. I will give them props for not being as overlydependant as current free-to-play games on mobile devices, but still is quite annoying.

Taken as a whole, I still would recommend play this game if you want to challenge yourself, and have quite a lot of time to spare inbetween life. If I were to give stars to rate the game overall, I would give this game a 3/5 stars overall.

It's not an easy product to review because it's not a game, but rather a launcher of several games (two at the time of writing) with different quality.

Haiku is my favourite developer of mobile "escape" games, which are more or less like hidden object games without hidden object puzzles. They've developed many excellent titles with action in modern times, something even Artifex Mundi failed to achieve in my opinion.

AEM is a straight forward mobile port and as such it comes with its all original limitations. It's f2p, but you need keys to unlock further chapters and you can only get them by paying or waiting 3h per key. This is not a welcome mechanics on PC and I hope it will be changed in the future. Personally I'd rather pay for each game and play whenever I want, perhaps each game could be a separate paid DLC for AEM which could stay free.

AEM comes with two games: Trapmaker and Pirate's Treasure. I enjoyed both on mobile, but I'm not sure if it was the best choice. Trapmaker is not the newest game and it shows unfortunately. Also Kate, the main character, makes several remarks to previous games, which won't be understood by new players. Pirate's Treasure, being a more modern title, seems much more polished and enjoyable to play, but I didn't find the main two characters to engaging.

A much better choice would be to launch AEM PC with Haiku's newest game The Covenant, which is a truly good, modern title. I'm sure this would attract many players.

I think it's still worth it to give AEM a try, but this is based more on what it can become based on the mobile version rather than what it is now on PC.

Adventure Escape Mysteries is a collection of what are essentially mass-produced mobile games. Haiku Games pumps out a few of these things a year, all with essentially the same format. They've been at it for about a decade now, and have produced over 30 games, the majority of which are included for free* in this collection.

The writing, art, and sound design are functional. They get the job done and nothing more, with the clear focus being to allow the developers to create the games cheaply and quickly. All of that is in service of the puzzles, which, speaking as someone who plays a lot of puzzle games, are solid and sometimes even ingenious. Don't let the packaging fool you: the puzzle quality is on par with what you might expect from more polished titles.

Now, on the asterisk. Each of the dozens of games included in this collection is divided into chapters, usually around 6-9, and each chapter might take anywhere from 20 minutes to an hour or so to play through. Chapters are unlocked with keys (one key per chapter). You get 1 key for free every 3 hours, and can hold up to 2 keys at a time (unless you purchase a larger bundle). Keys can be purchased to unlock chapters more quickly. You can also purchase stars, which can be used to buy hints, and which can also be earned by finding them hidden in games. There is one "Premium" game (so far) that can only be unlocked by purchasing it, and a few of the other games have bonus chapters that require a "VIP" purchase to unlock. Ultimately, that does amount to a lot of genuinely free content, depending on your level of patience.

The desktop version of AEM also comes with the benefit of not including in-game ads, like the mobile version does. It my opinion, that greatly improves the gaming experience. Though be warned I have run into a few (rare) puzzles that don't seem to be optimized for desktop and, as far as I can tell, cannot be completed without skipping them.

TLDR: A good way to scratch a puzzle game itch, with lots of free* content.

After what felt like an endless search, I finally found Adventure Escape Mysteries, a story-driven puzzle game that’s actually free to play! The game has a variety of stories, each with its own vibe—murder mysteries, supernatural adventures, you name it. I got so caught up in them; every story brings new characters and settings, which keeps things feeling fresh. The puzzles aren’t just random challenges either—they’re woven into the plot in a way that makes solving them feel rewarding and adds to the story’s momentum.

One of the best parts is that most stories are completely free, which is honestly hard to find in this kind of game. But heads-up: some premium stories do require a purchase to unlock. It can be a bit of a bummer if you’re hoping for everything to be free, but the quality and depth make it feel worth it to me. Plus, there’s so much free content that it doesn’t feel like you’re missing out if you decide not to pay.

Overall, I’d say Adventure Escape Mysteries finally delivers on the promise of a great, free story puzzle game. With its balance of engaging storytelling, cool art, and satisfying puzzles, it’s definitely worth downloading if you’re into mysteries and love solving problems!

Adventure Escape Mysteries is hours of good puzzles, fun stories, and cute graphics. This game is more of a package of a bunch of other games. Each story is fun, and the puzzles within them are different enough to make each game unique and enjoyable. Each story is made of multiple chapters, so there are plenty of puzzles to go around and lots of opportunities for fun.
The recurring characters and storylines are great. I love detective Kate, and have the most fun playing her stories. Different themed stories have different themed puzzles (even if the mechanics are similar), making each route entertaining in different ways. If you like mysteries, straightforward puzzle sequences, horror, or little romance novels, all those are included in these games. It's a really good bundle.
The key system is annoying but forgivable-- a key takes three hours to regenerate, which forces you to take breaks and not just power through the entire game. Unfortunately you can only have two keys at a time, though, so you can only ever really play two chapters at a time. I tend to play two to three sessions a day, so one story takes two to three days to complete. Thankfully once you complete a story it doesn't take any keys to replay, so achievement hunters need not worry about getting every star the first time through. This also means that there's replay-ability to the game-- beat a game once, leave the game in your library, and come back however much later and you can enjoy it again without the annoyance of the key system.

I know that there is a lot of criticism of the episodic nature of the games and the necessity to either wait for free episode keys to recharge or purchase them, but I have been happy to accept this in order to have access to so many games over time. I have only purchased a set of keys once (mainly as a "thank you" to the developers, to be honest), and usually I have been happy to go off and play another game or do something else entirely during the keys recharging period. I love point-and-click games. I love riddles, hidden objects and the entire atmosphere around it. So, on paper, I'm the perfect target for this game - and I can't lie, I had some fun at times. But there was something that bothered me, even in stories tagged as the easy mode: the absolute riddicoulness of some solutions. There are resolutions that you can't come up with without at least one hint from the game; if there's a code, you can be sure that you'll have to go back every stage to the place where the hint for the code was hidden because the game will never allow the character to write a note. More than once, I found myself searching up walkthroughs - something that rarely, if ever, happens for me while playing i.e. Axis Mundi point-n-click games.

Tired of that, I went back to Nightmares of the Deep trilogy - and it was only then, when I completed the game without a single search for herlp, when it hit me that "Adventure Escape Mysteries" are so depraved of logic because the devs want you to pay - not only for VIP stories or keys, but also for the damn stars. For me, the entire point of such games is to find solutions on my own, so this annoyed me. Enough to go against my perfectionist nature, and abandon this joke of a game despite not maxing the achievments. Also, it's a shitty move to involve paid achievments in a f2p game. Especially if you're translation to other languages sucks too, which shows absolute lack of care put into the game itself.

I so badly wanted to say this is good, but it just annoys me so much sometimes that it's lost all good faith I had. I don't care about the microtransactions (Escape Games are dip in games anyway and if you're stuck just use walkthroughs, save hint stars for skipping annoying puzzles) nor the episodes you need to buy (not that I'm happy about it, I came to 100% it and found out at least 9 achievements are locked behind a paywall. But so long as I get MOST of it, I can live with it at least). But the thing that makes me give this a bad review? The flip floppy nature of the puzzle difficulty. And no, I don't mean the fact it's "Beginner/Intermediate/Advanced", I mean the difficulty PER STORY.

Here's an example: I'm playing Death Dodgers. In one chapter, there's a puzzle where you count how many objects there are and that's the number on a code, one number for each code. The COLLECTIVE AMOUNT of this object equals the number (keep this in mind). Collective Amount codes are common fair in a lot of these puzzles. In the very next chapter, I see another puzzle with a similar motif: colour 1, colour 2, colour 3, colour 2, colour 1. I know images nearby have clues. Ergo, I do the usual, I add up the clues... Only it doesn't work. Nothing I can think of works. The answer, despite EVERY. SINGLE. GAME. I played THUS FAR (about 8 entire storylines) having "coloured things = collective number is code", this one is not that. This puzzle is "left number, left number, number, right number, right number".

And this isn't the first time the puzzle has been purposefully obtuse. People rip on Resident Evil for convoluted puzzles, but that's "use a thing, read a memo, find an object", they're basic. This? You can FEEL it was designed to force people to pay for hint stars. "The skeletons have directions on them", you mean the crook of the elbow that looks like an arrow for this arrow puzzle? "NO, MORON, IT'S THEIR NON-POINTY HANDS, OBVIOUSLY!". Not to mention, in Dark Ruins the rhythm game gives you notes that look exactly the same but one moves ahead of the other when you have two seconds to react and the forensics puzzle in Murder Inn has inaccurate readings. You know, forensics, the art of exact measurements, calculations and fact to determine who did what and how in law? Well, I got four different readings for the size of a bullet and the walkthrough I looked up showed a number I DIDN'T EVEN GET!!! It was a measuring tool WHICH MEASURED INCORRECTLY. And don't get me started on the fact that clicking an item will bring up a text box: You can't click anything pick-up-able while that text box is there. I clicked on the same god damn magnet 20 times and couldn't pick it up cos Kate yakked on about the board it was on. I solved the puzzle it was needed for with a little smarts (I tilted angled myself to see the outline of a creature in a fish tank then just tried the two possible combinations. Got it on the second one) but when I got bored of the tape puzzle that followed, went to a walkthrough to just get it out of the way, and then discovered you can, in fact, pick up the magnet, I was obviously aggravated.

Oh, but a time bomb? Getting shot at while pushing objects? Solving a puzzle that spanned an entire arcade? Piece of cake. All, btw, the final puzzle of the level. Same with the last Mirror Man puzzle. Same with Vanishing Act. Same with every. Single. Level. The annoying puzzles are the ones that are in the way, not the ones that matter. And I hate that the puzzles ruin this because there's glimmers of "Hey, that's a smart puzzle!", moments where the logic behind them is sound, where they do take some thinking but they're not impossible (again, even on Advanced, those difficulties mean nothing, puzzles flip flop). There's aspirations of a great Escape Game here, just like all the ones I played in the Flash era. Even the stories are good, I honestly like the writing and I was shocked to see so much death in these cos they give off the vibe of a teen game AT MOST, not something where you see a kid's parents die or a man turn into a skeleton.

But, no, the puzzles are clearly designed with hint money in mind. There's a difference between solving a Rubix Cube and solving it while on fire, blind, with your hands cut off, while falling off a cliff. And sadly the creators of these puzzles sometimes think the latter is the better choice...

Edit for later on: Having played more stories (as I mentioned, I'm achievement hunting), I am 100% firm in my belief they want your money, I found more purposefully obtuse puzzles and some broken ones too. Not broken as in unsolveable, broken as in the clues are practically useless to you and the instructions are so vague you may as well just say "Good luck, moron!" as a hint.

Edit two: Scratch that previous comment, one of the puzzles in final chapter of Cursed Crown is unplayable on PC cos it requires touch screen, so save 50 stars for that to skip it. I'm nearly done achievement hunting but, honestly, I think I'm put off Escape Games for life. I've reached a point of hate for these puzzles that I can totally understand why Bond villains would destroy the Earth over the pettiest of things. I don't want a gold star when I get a puzzle right, my reward will be never touching this ever again.

Edit three: I don't care if I don't have all the achievements (I'm not buying the Covenant nor playing this on mobile). I'm free! FREE, I TELL YOU! OH! It's so good to know I never need to touch this game again!
